title: The unification of humankind
note: Harari argues that history moves toward one connected world, bound by three unifiers: money, empires and universal religions. This is his framing. The economics of money and the dates of coinage are empirical, while his treatment of religion is an interpretation that many believers and scholars dispute.

read.title: Three roads to one world
text: Harari argues that history has a direction: small isolated groups merge into larger and larger networks until, in the modern era, humanity forms a single global system. He names three forces that pushed this along: money, empires and universal religions. This is his framework, and historians vary in how much weight they give each force.

Money is the easiest to check. It does three jobs: a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. Barter has a problem called the double coincidence of wants, since each trader must want what the other has. Money removes that problem. Harari adds that money works because strangers trust that others will accept it. Economists describe types of money, such as commodity money valued for its material and fiat money valued by government decree. The first stamped coins appeared in Lydia about 650 to 600 BCE, and paper money developed in Song China.

On empires, Harari defines them as political orders ruling many peoples with flexible borders, and notes that most people in history lived in them. On religion, he defines it broadly as a system of norms and values founded on belief in a superhuman order, and includes modern ideologies. That is a contested choice. Many scholars and believers argue that faith cannot be treated as a human-made order, and he is offering an interpretation, not a proven fact.
